item.title: Introduction
item.description: If you are completely new to LaTeX, I strongly recommend first looking at the LaTeX Basic Course. Many fundamental concepts will be used in this course, but not explained again.

item.title: Math Environments I
item.description:
As usual, the math side of LaTeX has two major parts: environments and commands.

The environments tell LaTeX: “hey, we want to go into math mode now” They also define some crucial overall functionality and layout to use in that mode.

item.title: Math Environments II
item.description: Last chapter discussed, among others, the displaymath and equation environment. Anywhere within these, you can use the sub environments I’ll discuss in this chapter.

item.title: Display Styles & Scripts
item.description: Earlier we saw two types of math environments: in line with the text (inline), or on its own line(s) (block).

item.title: Delimiters
item.description: Many mathematical formulas group their components with so-called delimiters. Think of regular arithmetic where 2*(5+6) is something different than (2*5)+6. But the uses go much further than that. For example, in computer science, you index the element of a list or array with [index].

item.title: Math Accents
item.description: You can’t blindly use text within a math environment like you normally would. This has been discussed numerous times now. That’s what makes this math mode special!

item.title: Functions
item.description: Any characters put into a math environment are displayed in an italic math font. Some operators though, mostly functions, are typically written with other letter styles. To make this efficient, these characters are provided as commands, simply by putting a \ in front of the regular function name.

item.title: Sums, Integrals & More
item.description: Some mathematical “functions” are so important (or just weird-looking) that tehy have their own special symbols and operators! These aren’t written by simply using their (shortened) name. This chapter discusses the most common ones: fractions, binomials, (square) roots, sums, products, integrals and logic/set operations.

item.title: Matrices
item.description: Using the delimiters seen before, you can already create matrices. Or, rather, things that look somewhat like a matrix.

item.title: Math Spacing & Special Text
item.description:
Before I throw all existing symbols at you, some slight important details warrant mentioning.

Within math environments, you can use the same spacing commands as anywhere else in LaTeX. But those are often too rough: within formulas, it’s about millimetres of added or removed space. Spacing is somewhat standardized, but also required to make the formulas easy to read and understand. Math is already complicated enough, at least we can try to typeset it cleanly.

item.title: Greek Symbols
item.description: Within mathematics, it’s common to use Greek letters for naming nearly everything. It’s useful, because they are easily recognizable, but don’t interfere with regular text. And not surprisingly, LaTeX has support for all the Greek symbols!

item.title: Math Symbols
item.description: I’ve already subtly mentioned that LaTeX uses a very complex set of rules to determine the amount of spacing around symbols.It also supports a humongous number of symbols.

item.title: Theorems & Proofs
item.description: Until now we’ve done everything inside math environments—which isn’t weird for a LaTeX Math course—but now it’s time to step out of it. Let’s look at mathematical concepts that don’t necessarily need to be formulas or equations. Common math concepts that don’t need to be in math mode.

item.title: Math Graphics
item.description: In the basic course we saw the command for including a picture file. It was \includegraphics. Which is slightly odd, isn’t it? Why not just use the simpler picture or graphics?

item.title: Conclusion
item.description:
Hopefully you now have the tools to typeset any (complicated) mathematics, formulas, algorithms and theorems you want.

Of course, there is way more available. More settings, more detailed commands, more packages to include that do fun stuff. But you won’t need them for 99% of the cases. LaTeX and math are already complicated enough, with many commands and operators to learn, so I wanted to keep the course to only the essentials.
